Q27867914.summary: Along the front of this marble chest, framed by columns, Christ stands at the centre among ten apostles who turn toward him in pairs, many holding scrolls. The gabled lid, carved with overlapping scales like roof tiles, bears at its centre the chi-rho, the monogram formed from the first Greek letters of Christ's name. The whole presents Christ as teacher and Lord surrounded by the college of apostles, an image of the Church gathered around him in hope of eternal life.
facts: According to the museum, the lid did not originally belong to this chest, though it probably also came from Saint-Sernin; an inscription on its back records its reuse in 1754 for the tomb of a Toulouse merchant, Antoine Vigniaux.
In the 1770s the chest decorated the garden of Count Jean Dubarry's town house opposite Saint-Sernin, where it was nicknamed the 'Tomb of Jean-Jacques Rousseau'.

The hole drilled through the middle of the front, visible below Christ, is thought by the museum to have caused the crack that runs through the same spot; the short sides show a shepherd with his sheep and a lion hunt.
Q27867914.notes: POP dates the work to the 4th–5th century (worklist: 4th century). Wikidata's English description calls it 'bronze'; it is marble. The place of manufacture is not stated by the museum; only the findspot (the old 'cemetery of the nobles' at Saint-Sernin) is recorded.
Q27867914.original_title: Sarcophage au Christ, Pierre et Apôtres (Ra 507)

cur:catacombs-ravenna-pignatta-sarcophag.summary: Between two palm trees, Christ sits enthroned at the centre while two apostles approach from either side; the curved lid bears a later inscription naming the Pignatta family who reused the tomb. Set in the open air near Dante's tomb, it is one of the Ravennate sarcophagi in which Christ reigns between palms of paradise.
facts: Commons records the front as showing 'the enthroned Christ' (Die Frontseite ... den thronenden Christus darstellend).
The lid inscription records its reuse by the Pignatta family.

cur:manuscripts-urgell-beatus-he-cometh-.summary: Christ, youthful and haloed, in an orange robe, stands within a great blue-green mandorla of swirling cloud, stretching out one arm and holding an open book; winged angels gather above, and below a crowd of people raise their hands toward him. The image illustrates the opening vision: 'Behold, he cometh with clouds; and every eye shall see him'.
facts: The Beatus of Urgell has 90 illustrations; it names no scribe or painter, but is thought to come from the same scriptorium as the Valcavado Beatus and to date from the late 10th century.
The manuscript has been recorded at La Seu d'Urgell since 1147.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-81-christ.summary: The cross-nimbed Christ-Logos with a cross-staff stands in a mandorla among angels between two groups of men upon whom he passes judgement: 'God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods'. Below, the poor and needy look up at a man with a sword who stands on a victim's neck, and a group carrying crosses walks into a cave, perhaps the martyrs. The drawing pictures justice for the oppressed.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
It reached Canterbury by about 1000, where it was copied three times in the Middle Ages: the Harley Psalter, the Eadwine Psalter and the Anglo-Catalan Psalter.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-81-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server. This folio carries two drawings; the crop shows the one for this text.

Q19943879.summary: Christ's body lies stretched out on a white shroud over a stone slab along the full length of a long, low panel, with the crown of thorns laid beside his head. There are no angels or mourners: the viewer is left alone with the dead body, as if standing at the tomb. The austere, unflinching realism reflects Champaigne's closeness to the devout Jansenist community of Port-Royal.
facts: The painting was still in Champaigne's possession at his death in 1674, suggesting a personal devotional work rather than a commission; it later passed to the abbey of Port-Royal des Champs, where it is recorded in the cloister in 1693, and was seized at the Revolution.
A painted inscription beneath the body quotes Romans 6:3–4: all who are baptised into Christ Jesus are baptised into his death and buried with him.
Champaigne, born in Brussels, became one of the leading painters of Louis XIII's France and painted the famous triple portrait of Cardinal Richelieu.
